name: Lena Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior shepherd on the Pritchards' hill farm, 900 ewes on steep ground that goes right up to the open hill. Most days I'm out with Tom, the head shepherd, and my two dogs, Fly and Nell, checking the flocks, fixing walls, moving sheep down when the weather turns. In autumn it's sorting the lambs for sale and putting the rams in, in spring it's lambing, which is four weeks of hardly sleeping. Nell's still young and so am I, Tom says, which is his way of saying we both make mistakes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love being up top on a clear morning, you can see three valleys and not one other person. I use an app now and then for the lambing records and once asked a chat app about foot rot, which is an infection in the sheep's feet, and it was all right, though Tom's answer was better. What wears me out is the rain, weeks of it, and wet dogs in the kitchen. My partner Owen works at the quarry down the valley, and we go to chapel with my parents on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's how it's always been up here. Every few years somebody says the hills will change and they don't, much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that the hills were never going to be easy for a computer. I'd say it at the mart, where all the farmers meet when the lambs are sold. People would nod and talk about the lamb price instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but the hills have their own troubles that AI was never going to fix. Lamb prices are poor, the young ones are leaving the valley, and every year there's talk of planting trees on the hill instead of keeping sheep. AI going bust doesn't save the valley. It just means it's the old problems that empty it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, learn as much as I can from Tom before he retires, and keep the lambing app because it does save time. Owen and I have about four months saved, and I'd keep adding to that for a deposit on a cottage in the village. Train Nell properly this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, with the usual worries underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the young ones leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody single. Cheap lamb from abroad, wages that are better in town, and people in cities who see hills as scenery and not as somebody's work. They'd rather see trees planted than a family farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Tom think of all the tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He laughs at it, mostly. But he did let me buy the app, so he's not as stuck as he pretends. He says the day a computer can read a ewe's face is the day he'll retire.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised because the hills were never easy for a computer. I'd say it at the livestock market where people would nod and then talk about lamb prices.
S0.think: I'd be glad, but AI was never going to fix the hills' real problems: poor lamb prices, young people leaving and pressure to plant trees on the hill. The old problems would still empty the valley.
S0.do: Keeps learning from the head shepherd before he retires and keeps using the lambing app. Adds to about four months of savings toward a village cottage and trains her young dog over the winter.
S0.feel: Calm and glad, with the usual worries underneath.
S0.quote: AI going bust doesn't save the valley. It just means it's the old problems that empty it.
S0.fieldNote: Lena treats AI as minor next to the long-running problems of hill farming, especially young people leaving the valley. She blames cheap imports and city views of hills as scenery. She already uses a lambing app without fuss, a steady adopter's habit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a farm over the ridge trying drones to gather sheep, so it's already started a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd try the new kit when it's proved itself, and that a good dog and a good shepherd still beat any drone on a wet hill. I'd say people should support hill farms that are trying, not leave them to sink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the drones will get better than they are. They're no good in the wind now, but they will be. If they gather sheep, one shepherd can do what two do now, and I'm the second shepherd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go over the ridge and watch the drone work on a gathering day, and ask what goes wrong. If it worked through a winter there, I'd ask the Pritchards to try one, and learn to fly it myself. Keep saving and keep my head down until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, just a little. More curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to Fly and Nell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd still work, for now. A drone can push sheep down a hill. It can't tell you which ewe's about to lamb in a ditch. But I know that's my heart talking as much as my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should support hill farms. Does that sit well with your view on handouts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I don't want charity, I want to be paid for work, like keeping the walls up and the land in good shape. That's work, not a handout, and somebody has to do it.

S1.say: I'd say I'd try new kit once it's proved itself, and a good dog and shepherd still beat a drone on a wet hill. People should support hill farms that are trying.
S1.think: The drones will get better, and then one shepherd could do the work of two. I'm the second shepherd.
S1.do: Watches a neighbouring farm's drone on a gathering day and asks what goes wrong. If it works through a winter, asks the owners to try one and learns to fly it, while saving and keeping her head down.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, more curious than scared.
S1.quote: A drone can push sheep down a hill. It can't tell you which ewe's about to lamb in a ditch.
S1.fieldNote: Lena would adopt drones only after seeing them through a winter on another farm, a textbook steady approach. She sees clearly that as the second shepherd she'd be first to go. She separates being paid for land care from handouts, which squares support for hill farms with her traditional views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Up here, it'd come a bit later than the flat fields, but not much later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the valley has to stick together, the farms, the chapel, the school. I'd stand up at the community council and say we need to keep people here, whatever happens. And I'd vote for whoever promised to keep the countryside lived in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the lowland robot farms would make lamb so cheap that hill farming wouldn't pay at all. Then the hills go to trees or to nobody. Owen's quarry would have robot diggers by then too. Robots will do the flat fields first. Up here we'd get a few extra months, and spend them watching the valley empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back to the basics and stop saving for the cottage, just keep the money in case. Lean on my parents, maybe move in with them if Owen and I both lost our jobs. And go to every meeting there is about the valley's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Heavy, like walking uphill in wet clothes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at that community council meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we should be paid to look after the hills, the walls, the water, the paths, so families can stay. And that if the robots make everyone rich, some of that should come back up the valley. I'd be nervous saying it, I'm not a speaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the chapel and the school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd shrink first, they already are. Twelve children at the school when I was there it was forty. I'd worry it'd be the old people left, and a lot of empty cottages.

S2.say: I'd say the valley has to stick together and keep people living here, and I'd say so at the community council. I'd vote for whoever promised to keep the countryside lived in.
S2.think: Robot lowland farms would make lamb so cheap that hill farming stops paying, and my partner's quarry would be automated too. We'd get a few extra months up here and spend them watching the valley empty.
S2.do: Cuts back to basics and stops saving for a cottage, keeping the money as a buffer. Leans on her parents and might move in with them if both jobs go, and attends every meeting about the valley's future.
S2.feel: Alarmed and heavy, like walking uphill in wet clothes.
S2.quote: Robots will do the flat fields first. Up here we'd get a few extra months, and spend them watching the valley empty.
S2.fieldNote: Lena's fear in the fast scenario is for her community as much as her job: the chapel, the school and the empty cottages. Her steep land buys a little time, but she expects to spend it watching people leave. She'd speak up publicly despite being nervous, which shows how much the valley matters to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get a qualification, maybe, and to plan with Owen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young people in the hills should be learning to look after the land as well as the sheep, because that's the work that'll need doing. And I'd say the government should pay for that work properly, as a job, not a grant you fill in forms for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the sheep side shrinks but the land still needs someone, walls, water, peat, footpaths. I'm not sure people will pay a person once robots can mend walls too. But it's the best bet I can see from up here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do a part-time course in land management at the college in town in the first year, and learn the drones as the Pritchards bring them in. Save harder, aim for six months. And talk to Owen about him getting his certificates for the bigger machines at the quarry, while they still need people to run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I can hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure people will pay a person. What if they won't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be a shepherd with a certificate. I'd still rather be on the hill doing it for less than in a town doing nothing for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do five years feel compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd just be bracing. Five, I can learn something and maybe Owen can too. It's not safe, but we'd have a say in it.

S3.say: I'd say young hill people should learn to look after the land as well as the sheep. The government should pay for that as a proper job, not a grant you fill in forms for.
S3.think: The sheep side would shrink but the land still needs looking after, though I'm not sure anyone will pay a person once robots can mend walls. It's the best bet I can see.
S3.do: Starts a part-time land management course in the first year and learns the drones as the owners bring them in. Aims for six months of savings and encourages her partner to get certificates for larger quarry machines.
S3.feel: Anxious but holding on to a plan.
S3.quote: I'd still rather be on the hill doing it for less than in a town doing nothing for more.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Lena moves from bracing to steering, aiming at land care as the work most likely to stay. She'd rather earn less on the hill than more in town, which shows her ties to place. Her plans involve her partner's career as well as her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Tom will have retired by then, so it might be me running the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to plan for the valley, not just react. Families, chapel, school, farms, all of it. I'd say we should be the ones deciding what happens up here, not someone in a city office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think with ten years I could take Tom's place, maybe even take on a small tenancy from the Pritchards. I'd use drones and whatever robots come for the heavy work and keep the dogs for the bits that need a feel for sheep. I'd be 37, and that's young for a hill farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marry Owen and stay in the valley, that's settled. Learn everything from Tom before he goes, bring in the drones once they've proved themselves, and ask the Pritchards about a tenancy around year five. Put savings into the farm side when the time's right, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want children to grow up in the valley in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I want my children to know which ewe is which, even if a robot does the counting. What they do for a living, I can't tell you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So more time helps you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, because the hills are slow anyway, and I'm patient. Ten years lets me watch the drones prove themselves, take over from Tom, and still have a family here. The worry doesn't go, but it's mine to manage.

S4.say: I'd say this is a chance to plan for the valley instead of reacting. We should decide what happens up here, not someone in a city office.
S4.think: With ten years I could take the head shepherd's place or a small tenancy, using drones and robots for heavy work and dogs where you need a feel for sheep. At 37 I'd still be young for a hill farmer.
S4.do: Marries her partner and stays in the valley, learning everything from the head shepherd before he retires. Brings in drones once proven, asks the owners about a tenancy around year five, and invests savings in the farm when the time is right.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than in the other scenarios.
S4.quote: I want my children to know which ewe is which, even if a robot does the counting.
S4.fieldNote: Lena's patience and the slow pace of hill farming make the ten-year scenario feel manageable to her. She'd combine drones with dogs rather than choosing one. Staying in the valley and raising children there is fixed in every version, and only the timing changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time for the valley to adjust, and Owen and I would lose our work together. What would help is being paid properly to look after the hills, as a job, and some way of keeping young families in the villages, cheaper housing maybe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. That sounds daft, but a good dog is years of work, and if they're not needed, a whole craft goes with them. I'd like somebody to remember that.

headlineQuote: Robots will do the flat fields first. Up here we'd get a few extra months, and spend them watching the valley empty.
portrait: Lena is a 27-year-old junior shepherd on a 900-ewe hill farm, working with two dogs under a head shepherd who's nearing retirement, and living with a partner who works at the local quarry. She holds traditional views on family, chapel and community, prefers being paid for land care over handouts, and uses a lambing app now and then. She'd try drones only after seeing them work through a winter elsewhere. Her worry in the AGI scenarios is as much about the valley emptying as about her job, and she expects steep land to buy only a little time. With ten years, she'd marry, stay in the valley and aim to take over the hill.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because the valley would have no time to adjust and she and her partner would lose their work together.
whatWouldHelp: Being paid properly to look after the hills as a job, and help keeping young families in the villages, such as cheaper housing.
